title: The jobs employers expect to shrink by 2030 (and what to do instead)
text:
Employers expect bank tellers, data entry clerks, postal service clerks, cashiers, administrative assistants, and accountants and auditors to be among the fastest-declining jobs by 2030, while big data, fintech, AI and machine learning, software and security roles grow fastest (World Economic Forum, Future of Jobs Report 2025).

And about 60% of US jobs are types of work created since 1940 (MIT research, Quarterly Journal of Economics). New work keeps being invented, so the job you'll love might not have a name yet. Don't choose a job title. Find the kind of work you're good at, then test it.

title: 39% of your skills will change by 2030. So what should you learn?
text:
Workers can expect 39% of their existing skill sets to be transformed or become outdated between 2025 and 2030, and if the world's workforce were 100 people, 59 would need training by 2030 (World Economic Forum, Future of Jobs Report 2025).

So what should you learn? The skill that doesn't expire is finding out, fast, what you're good at. Before you pay for a course, try an hour of the real work. Then decide.

title: AI CEOs can't agree what happens to jobs. Here's what to do anyway
text:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned AI could wipe out about half of all entry-level white-collar jobs (Axios interview, May 2025). Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang: "Some jobs will be obsolete, but many jobs are going to be created." (VivaTech, June 2025)

The people building AI can't agree, so nobody knows yet. But one thing is already happening: AI changes the tasks inside a job before it changes the job title. So audit one week: mark every block as cheap to produce or hard to replace. Then test one direction next to yours, before you need to.

title: Nvidia's CEO: you won't lose your job to AI. You'll lose it to this
text:
"You're not going to lose your job to an AI, but you're going to lose your job to someone who uses AI." Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Milken Institute Global Conference, May 2025.

So become that someone. Try the 80% test this week: give AI the most repetitive task in your week, let it draft the first 80%, and write down everything you had to fix. That list is where your value sits.

Some people are turning that list into a job: AI workflow designers redesign how a team works once part of the work can go to a model, and model evaluation writers design the tests that show whether an AI is good enough, and where it fails. title: Microsoft ranked 785 jobs by AI overlap. Is yours top 10?
text:
Microsoft Research studied 200,000 real conversations with its AI (Bing Copilot) and scored 785 US jobs by how much their work overlaps with what AI already does. The top 10: interpreters and translators, historians, writers and authors, services sales reps, CNC tool programmers, broadcast announcers and radio DJs, customer service reps, telemarketers, political scientists and mathematicians. Software developers come 120th.

What it doesn't mean: that these jobs are disappearing. The researchers say reading the scores as job loss "would be a mistake", and the #1 job, interpreters and translators, is still projected to grow 2% in the US from 2025 to 2035 (the average job: 3%). Hot isn't cooked. Tasks change before titles do.

title: Is a computer science degree cooked? (NY Fed data)
text:
Recent computer science grads (ages 22 to 27) had the 4th-highest unemployment rate of 73 majors in 2024: 7.0%, against 4.2% for all recent grads. That's higher than art history (6.7%), English (6.1%) and philosophy (5.1%).

But only 19% of CS grads work in jobs that don't need a degree (all recent grads: 39%), and US software developer jobs are projected to grow 10% from 2025 to 2035 (the average job: 3%). Our read: not cooked, but harder to get into. So don't just collect the degree. Build proof: ship one real project a month, get good at checking AI's code, and test a direction next to yours.
